title: KML Named Placemark Counter: Label Coverage
description: Count KML Placemarks that carry their own name with the KML Named Placemark Counter — audit label coverage before you share a file. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a file with 120 Placemarks of which 96 carry a direct <name> has 80% label coverage — and the 24 anonymous ones are exactly what this audit finds before your client does.
quick_answer: The KML Named Placemark Counter counts the Placemarks in a KML file that carry their own direct <name> element, and compares them with the total — an audit of label coverage. Drop the file and read how many features will actually be labelled when the file is opened, computed locally.

examples.label: Example · Direct name versus inherited name

body.t: A Placemark inside a named Folder is still unnamed if it lacks its own <name> — Earth shows the folder's organisation, not a label for the point. This counter follows the strict rule: the Placemark's own direct child or it does not count.
A GIS export stores the label in <ExtendedData><Data name='Label'>. Rich in the source system, invisible as a name in KML viewers. Coverage here: 0% named — correctly, painfully, usefully.

faq: What counts as a name, exactly?

A <name> element that is a direct child of the <Placemark>. Names inherited from folders, stored in descriptions or held in ExtendedData do not count — the audit measures labels as viewers render them.
A <name></name> with no text names nothing. It is an element, not a label — treated as unnamed by any honest reading, this one included.
Placemark is the feature unit; its geometry type does not affect naming. Every Placemark is audited for its own name.
What is a good coverage target?
For delivered map files: 100% for features a reader must identify, and a stated reason for any exception. The audit makes the gap list; the target is your professional call.
Technically text, practically anonymous. The counter counts characters honestly; your QA eye should not.
That names the file, not its features — excluded, correctly.
Why not credit description-first-text as a label?
Because viewers do not render it as one. An audit that flatters the file helps nobody when the client opens it.
